priorityReading.title: Effect of a home-based calf neuromuscular electrical stimulation programme on walking capacity in adults with lower-extremity peripheral artery disease: the ELECTRO-PAD RCT.
priorityReading.abstract:
AIMS: This study aims to evaluate whether a 3-month home-based neuromuscular electrical stimulation (NMES) programme improved maximal walking distance (MWD) in patients with lower-extremity peripheral artery disease (PAD) compared with usual care.

METHODS AND RESULTS: This multicentre randomized clinical trial included 73 adults with PAD and walking impairment from five French university hospitals between September 2019 and July 2022, with final follow-up in November 2022. Participants were randomized to a NMES group (n = 34) or a usual care group (n = 39) for 3 months. Both groups received standard medical management and lifestyle advice; the NMES group performed calf NMES sessions at home for 2-3 h/day, 5 days/week. The primary outcome was the 3-month change in treadmill MWD. Secondary outcomes included change in 6-min total walking distance. Of the 73 randomized participants [mean (SD) age, 62.8 (9.2) years; 14 (19.2%) women], 64 (88%) completed the 3-month follow-up. Mean treadmill MWD increased from 148.5 m at baseline to 254.1 m at 3 months in the NMES group and from 142.5 to 175.8 m in the usual care group [between-group difference, 69.9 m (95% CI, 10.8-129.0 m); P = 0.02]. The 6-min total walking distance improved from 371.0 to 405.4 m with NMES and from 342.5 to 348.8 m with usual care [between-group difference, 29.6 m (95% CI, 5.1-54.1 m); P = 0.02].

CONCLUSION: In patients with PAD and walking impairment, a 3-month home-based calf NMES programme significantly improved walking capacity. Further studies are needed to assess long-term effects.

REGISTRATION: ClinicalTrials.gov identifier: NCT03795103.

LAY SUMMARY: This study found that using a small electrical stimulation device at home for 3 months (2-3 h/day, 5 days/week) helped people with lower-extremity peripheral artery disease walk farther than those receiving only usual care including usual medical treatment and a brochure with general advice for an active lifestyle.Participants who used the device walked about 70 m farther on a treadmill than those who did not.They also improved their 6-min walking distance by about 30 m and tended to increase their daily physical activity level.

priorityReading.title: Beyond injury grade: Anatomic location and outcomes after endovascular repair of blunt thoracic aortic injury.
priorityReading.abstract:
OBJECTIVE: Contemporary risk stratification for blunt thoracic aortic injury (BTAI) has largely emphasized injury grade, whereas the prognostic importance of injury location remains poorly defined. More proximal injuries may require complex arch reconstruction and management of the supra-aortic branches, potentially increasing procedural risk. We evaluated the association between anatomic aortic injury zone and perioperative and long-term outcomes after thoracic endovascular aortic repair (TEVAR).

METHODS: We performed a retrospective cohort study of patients undergoing TEVAR for BTAI in the Society for Vascular Surgery Vascular Quality Initiative from 2013 through April 1, 2026. Patients were classified according to the proximal extent of the aortic injury as proximal (zones 0-2), isthmic (zone 3), or distal (zones 4-5). Multinomial propensity scores incorporating pretreatment demographic, comorbidity, physiologic, and injury-severity variables were used to generate stabilized inverse probability of treatment weights. Weighted logistic regression with center-clustered standard errors evaluated perioperative outcomes. Cox regression evaluated all-cause mortality, and Fine-Gray regression evaluated aorta- or branch-related reintervention with death treated as a competing event. Zone 3 served as the reference group.

RESULTS: Among 2,693 patients, 551 (20.5%) had proximal injuries, 1,772 (65.8%) had zone 3 injuries, and 370 (13.7%) had distal injuries. Injury-grade distributions did not differ significantly among groups. After weighting, proximal injury was associated with greater in-hospital mortality compared with zone 3 injury (11.0% vs. 8.5%; odds ratio [OR], 1.33; 95% confidence interval [CI], 1.01-1.76; P=0.046) and greater 30-day aortic reintervention (2.2% vs. 0.8%; OR, 3.00; 95% CI, 1.30-6.92; P=0.010). Stroke and spinal cord ischemia did not differ significantly. Proximal injury was also associated with a greater cumulative incidence of aortic reintervention (subdistribution hazard ratio, 1.94; 95% CI, 1.06-3.53; P=0.031), although its association with all-cause mortality during follow-up did not reach statistical significance (hazard ratio, 1.28; 95% CI, 0.99-1.65; P=0.060). Distal injury was not associated with increased perioperative or long-term adverse outcomes compared with zone 3 injury.

CONCLUSIONS: Among patients undergoing TEVAR for BTAI, proximal injury location was associated with greater in-hospital mortality and aortic reintervention despite similar injury-grade distributions. Anatomic injury zone may complement injury grade when assessing procedural risk and planning postoperative surveillance.

priorityReading.title: Comprehensive risk factor control in Type 2 diabetes and incident peripheral artery disease.
priorityReading.abstract:
AIMS: Patients with Type 2 diabetes (T2D) are at an elevated risk of peripheral artery disease (PAD) compared with the general population. This study aimed to investigate whether joint risk factor control could mitigate the T2D-related excess risk of PAD.

METHODS AND RESULTS: This study included 14 458 participants with T2D who were initially free of cardiovascular disease and PAD and matched them with 56 961 control individuals from the UK Biobank cohort. Participants with T2D were categorized according to the number of risk factors controlled, including no current smoking, being physically active, healthy diet, and guideline-recommended levels of glycated haemoglobin, body mass index, blood pressure, LDL cholesterol, and urinary albumin. During a median follow-up of 11.9 years, 408 (2.8%) participants with T2D and 671 (1.2%) matched non-T2D individuals developed PAD. Among participants with T2D, a greater number of controlled risk factors were associated with lower PAD incidence (∼23% lower risk per additional factor). Compared with the matched non-T2D individuals, the hazard ratio [95% confidence interval (CI)] for PAD among participants with T2D gradually decreased from 2.49 (1.94, 3.19) for those with ≤2 risk factors controlled to 0.82 (0.51, 1.31) for those with ≥6 risk factors controlled. At 45 years of age, the difference in PAD-free survival time was on average -1.41 (95% CI -1.78, -1.03) years for participants with T2D who had ≤2 risk factors controlled and -0.11 (95% CI -0.38, 0.16) years for those who had ≥6 risk factors controlled compared with the non-T2D individuals.

CONCLUSION: Individuals with T2D who achieved optimal risk factor control had no excess risk of PAD than matched non-T2D counterparts. Efforts to promote comprehensive risk factor management in T2D are imperative for reducing the burden of PAD.

priorityReading.title: Global, regional, and national perspectives on aortic aneurysm burden from 1992 to 2021: temporal patterns and age-period-cohort analyses.
priorityReading.abstract:
AIMS: To assess the global, regional, and country-specific trends in the burden of Aortic aneurysm (AA) from 1992 to 2021, with a focus on mortality rates, disability-adjusted life-years (DALYs), and socio-demographic inequalities.

METHODS AND RESULTS: The Global Burden of Disease (GBD) 2021 study data were utilized to calculate the age-standardized mortality rates (ASMR) and disability-adjusted life-year rates (ASDR) for AA in 204 countries. Temporal patterns were assessed using Joinpoint regression and age-period-cohort modelling. Cross-country inequalities were evaluated using the slope index of inequality (SII) and concentration index. Globally, the disease burden of AA showed a downward trend. The ASMR for AA decreased from 2.57 per 100 000 (95% uncertainty interval (UI): 2.37, 2.72) in 1992 to 1.86 per 100 000 (95% UI: 1.67, 2.00) in 2021 (EAPC: -1.36%). The age effect indicated that the age-specific mortality rate sharply escalates with age, but opposite trends exist in period and cohort effects. The gender-specific analysis confirmed a consistently higher burden in males, with more pronounced reductions in high socio-demographic index (SDI) regions. Cross-country analyses highlighted widening absolute inequalities (SII: 74.4 to 84.1) but reduced relative inequalities (concentration index: 0.48 to 0.28) over time.

CONCLUSION: There is a downward trend in the global burden of AA from 1992 to 2021, with significant disparities observed across genders, age groups, and SDI regions. These findings emphasize the need for prevention through base healthcare services, risk factor management, and equitable access to interventions to effectively address the disproportionate AA burden.

priorityReading.title: Wider social determinants of the presentation and outcomes of patients enrolled in small abdominal aortic aneurysm surveillance.
priorityReading.abstract:
OBJECTIVE: Elective repair offers better outcomes than urgent repair for patients in small abdominal aortic aneurysm (AAA) surveillance who reach treatment thresholds, or treatment being declined due to surgical risk. Internationally, socioeconomically deprived, ethnic minority, and rural populations receive fewer guideline recommended surgical procedures. In Aotearoa New Zealand (NZ), Māori face barriers to timely surgical access. This multicentre, observational analysis of prospectively collected AAA surveillance data (2002 - 2019) examined disparities in AAA stage at diagnosis and elective repair by socioeconomic deprivation, ethnicity, and distance to vascular services.

METHODS: Patients with incidentally detected AAAs were grouped by socioeconomic deprivation, ethnicity (Māori/non-Māori), and travel time to vascular services. Outcomes included age and AAA diameter at diagnosis, and elective repair rates. Cumulative incidence functions estimated 36 month probability of elective repair, with cause specific Cox regression adjusted for comorbidities.

RESULTS: 1 684 patients were eligible for analysis. Patients in highly deprived areas were diagnosed younger, but higher deprivation was associated with lower elective repair rates (hazard ratio [HR] 0.85, 95% confidence interval [CI] 0.75 - 0.98; p = .02). Māori were diagnosed younger (68.7 vs. 73.4 years; p < .001) yet had lower elective repair rates for medium (≥ 45 mm) AAAs in univariable analysis (36 month probability 0.27 vs. 0.54; p = .04) and multivariable analysis controlling for covariates (HR 0.51, 95% CI 0.29 - 0.86; p = .01) despite reaching treatment thresholds at least as often. Rural location was not associated with repair rates.

CONCLUSION: Socioeconomic and ethnic inequities in outcomes of small AAA surveillance exist in NZ. Patients in more deprived areas had lower elective repair rates. Māori received fewer elective repairs despite equivalent or greater clinical need, likely reflecting higher comorbidity burden and operative risk. Earlier diagnosis, improved access to specialist care, including national AAA screening, enhanced risk factor management, and strengthened primary care access may reduce inequity. Socioeconomic, ethnic, and geographical factors should inform equitable screening and service delivery.

priorityReading.title: Efficacy and safety of variable perioperative antiplatelet regimens in patients undergoing carotid endarterectomy.
priorityReading.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Current SVS recommendations for perioperative antithrombotic therapy in patients undergoing carotid endarterectomy (CEA) are limited. In acutely symptomatic patients, dual antiplatelet therapy (DAPT) is recommended for secondary stroke prevention. In asymptomatic patients, there are no clear recommendations, though single antiplatelet therapy with aspirin (ASA) is commonly used. We examined the efficacy and safety of various perioperative antiplatelet regimens in patients who underwent CEA in the VQI.

METHODS: We retrospectively reviewed all patients who underwent CEA in VQI from January 2003 to September 2024. We stratified patients based on their pre-operative antiplatelet regimen: No-antiplatelet, ASA-only, Clopidogrel-only, DAPT (ASA/Clopidogrel), and Alternative-DAPT (ASA/Alternative P2Y12 Inhibitors). We created propensity scores for each treatment regimen and assessed in-hospital stroke/death and bleeding complications using inverse probability of treatment weighted log binomial regression, with ASA-only as the reference group and adjusting for intraoperative protamine use and drain placement. We also assessed outcomes stratified by preoperative symptom status.

RESULTS: Of 195,619 CEA patients: 53% received ASA-only, 11% No-antiplatelet, 6% Clopidogrel-only, 30% DAPT, and 1% Alternative-DAPT. The corresponding unadjusted rates of in-hospital stroke/death were 1.3%, 1.7%, 1.2%, 1.2%, and 1.6%. After adjustment, compared with ASA-only, in-hospital stroke/death was lower with Clopidogrel-only (RR 0.81, 95% CI 0.67-0.97) and DAPT (RR 0.79, 95% CI 0.72-0.87). In symptomatic patients (26% of the cohort), there was a trend towards lower in-hospital stroke/death with DAPT (RR 0.88, 95% CI 0.76-1.00). In asymptomatic patients, in-hospital stroke/death was lower with Clopidogrel-only (RR 0.69, 95% CI 0.52-0.90) and DAPT (RR 0.73, 95% CI 0.64-0.83). Bleeding complications were higher with DAPT (RR 1.49, 95% CI 1.35-1.66) and trended toward higher with Clopidogrel-only (RR 1.22, 95% CI 1.00-1.48) but were similar across other regimens.

CONCLUSIONS: Compared with ASA-monotherapy, Clopidogrel-monotherapy and DAPT were associated with lower rates of in-hospital stroke/death after CEA driven by lower rates of stroke, albeit with higher rates of bleeding complications, particularly with DAPT. These findings highlight Clopidogrel-monotherapy as a potential alternative to DAPT for patients undergoing CEA, with similar efficacy and more acceptable bleeding risk. Analyses in patients on alternative P2Y12 inhibitors were limited by sample size; however, analyses with a larger cohort will be valuable in the future. Overall, our findings emphasize a potential role for clopidogrel-monotherapy in stroke prevention among patients undergoing CEA and highlight the importance of individualized risk assessment.

priorityReading.title: Predicting Morbidity, Mortality, Revision, and Ambulation in Patients Undergoing Major Lower Limb Amputation for Peripheral Arterial Disease or Diabetes Mellitus: The Case for Regional Level Clinical Prediction Models.
priorityReading.abstract:
OBJECTIVE: Several outcome prediction tools exist to support decision making for patients undergoing major lower limb amputation (MLLA). However, most predict a single outcome, are derived from registry level data, and lack external validation. The present study aimed to develop clinically focussed, multi-outcome prediction tools using granular regional data with immediate external validation on an international database.

METHODS: This study involved development, and internal and external validation of multivariable binomial and multinomial regression prediction models. All patients undergoing MLLA for ischaemic or diabetic indications between 1 January 2013 and 1 July 2023 at a single regional vascular hub were used for model development. Clinically focussed logistic multivariable binomial and multinomial regression models were developed predicting 30 day and 1 year mortality and revision, 30 day major morbidity or mortality, and best mobility achieved (binary and 3 category). Model complexity, crossvalidated receiver operating curve (ROC) discrimination and calibration were assessed and optimised, with the best performing models undergoing external validation on PERCEIVE study data. External validity was assessed using discrimination and calibration statistics, with one revision attempt permitted.

RESULTS: The development dataset included 609 patients (75.2% men, median age 69 years). Internal crossvalidated ROC values were 0.774 for 30 day mortality, 0.752 for 1 year mortality, 0.679 for 30 day revision, 0.707 for 1 year revision, 0.699 for 30 day major morbidity or mortality, 0.876 for binary best ambulation, and 0.752 for 3 category best ambulation predictions. All models were well calibrated. On external validation the ROC values were 0.616, 0.722, 0.617, 0.488, 0.697, 0.643, and 0.602, respectively.

CONCLUSION: The prediction models performed well for internal "regional" patient outcomes, especially for mortality and ambulation. On external validation, like other models externally validated on the PERCEIVE data, they failed to generalise to the wider population undergoing MLLA, except for 1 year mortality. Predicting patient outcomes from pre-operative variables remains challenging; however, regional level modelling may provide better performance over more general prediction tools.

priorityArticles.title: Global, regional, and national perspectives on aortic aneurysm burden from 1992 to 2021: temporal patterns and age-period-cohort analyses.
priorityArticles.abstract:
AIMS: To assess the global, regional, and country-specific trends in the burden of Aortic aneurysm (AA) from 1992 to 2021, with a focus on mortality rates, disability-adjusted life-years (DALYs), and socio-demographic inequalities.

METHODS AND RESULTS: The Global Burden of Disease (GBD) 2021 study data were utilized to calculate the age-standardized mortality rates (ASMR) and disability-adjusted life-year rates (ASDR) for AA in 204 countries. Temporal patterns were assessed using Joinpoint regression and age-period-cohort modelling. Cross-country inequalities were evaluated using the slope index of inequality (SII) and concentration index. Globally, the disease burden of AA showed a downward trend. The ASMR for AA decreased from 2.57 per 100 000 (95% uncertainty interval (UI): 2.37, 2.72) in 1992 to 1.86 per 100 000 (95% UI: 1.67, 2.00) in 2021 (EAPC: -1.36%). The age effect indicated that the age-specific mortality rate sharply escalates with age, but opposite trends exist in period and cohort effects. The gender-specific analysis confirmed a consistently higher burden in males, with more pronounced reductions in high socio-demographic index (SDI) regions. Cross-country analyses highlighted widening absolute inequalities (SII: 74.4 to 84.1) but reduced relative inequalities (concentration index: 0.48 to 0.28) over time.

CONCLUSION: There is a downward trend in the global burden of AA from 1992 to 2021, with significant disparities observed across genders, age groups, and SDI regions. These findings emphasize the need for prevention through base healthcare services, risk factor management, and equitable access to interventions to effectively address the disproportionate AA burden.

priorityArticles.title: Wider social determinants of the presentation and outcomes of patients enrolled in small abdominal aortic aneurysm surveillance.
priorityArticles.abstract:
OBJECTIVE: Elective repair offers better outcomes than urgent repair for patients in small abdominal aortic aneurysm (AAA) surveillance who reach treatment thresholds, or treatment being declined due to surgical risk. Internationally, socioeconomically deprived, ethnic minority, and rural populations receive fewer guideline recommended surgical procedures. In Aotearoa New Zealand (NZ), Māori face barriers to timely surgical access. This multicentre, observational analysis of prospectively collected AAA surveillance data (2002 - 2019) examined disparities in AAA stage at diagnosis and elective repair by socioeconomic deprivation, ethnicity, and distance to vascular services.

METHODS: Patients with incidentally detected AAAs were grouped by socioeconomic deprivation, ethnicity (Māori/non-Māori), and travel time to vascular services. Outcomes included age and AAA diameter at diagnosis, and elective repair rates. Cumulative incidence functions estimated 36 month probability of elective repair, with cause specific Cox regression adjusted for comorbidities.

RESULTS: 1 684 patients were eligible for analysis. Patients in highly deprived areas were diagnosed younger, but higher deprivation was associated with lower elective repair rates (hazard ratio [HR] 0.85, 95% confidence interval [CI] 0.75 - 0.98; p = .02). Māori were diagnosed younger (68.7 vs. 73.4 years; p < .001) yet had lower elective repair rates for medium (≥ 45 mm) AAAs in univariable analysis (36 month probability 0.27 vs. 0.54; p = .04) and multivariable analysis controlling for covariates (HR 0.51, 95% CI 0.29 - 0.86; p = .01) despite reaching treatment thresholds at least as often. Rural location was not associated with repair rates.

CONCLUSION: Socioeconomic and ethnic inequities in outcomes of small AAA surveillance exist in NZ. Patients in more deprived areas had lower elective repair rates. Māori received fewer elective repairs despite equivalent or greater clinical need, likely reflecting higher comorbidity burden and operative risk. Earlier diagnosis, improved access to specialist care, including national AAA screening, enhanced risk factor management, and strengthened primary care access may reduce inequity. Socioeconomic, ethnic, and geographical factors should inform equitable screening and service delivery.

priorityArticles.title: Efficacy and safety of variable perioperative antiplatelet regimens in patients undergoing carotid endarterectomy.
priorityArticles.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Current SVS recommendations for perioperative antithrombotic therapy in patients undergoing carotid endarterectomy (CEA) are limited. In acutely symptomatic patients, dual antiplatelet therapy (DAPT) is recommended for secondary stroke prevention. In asymptomatic patients, there are no clear recommendations, though single antiplatelet therapy with aspirin (ASA) is commonly used. We examined the efficacy and safety of various perioperative antiplatelet regimens in patients who underwent CEA in the VQI.

METHODS: We retrospectively reviewed all patients who underwent CEA in VQI from January 2003 to September 2024. We stratified patients based on their pre-operative antiplatelet regimen: No-antiplatelet, ASA-only, Clopidogrel-only, DAPT (ASA/Clopidogrel), and Alternative-DAPT (ASA/Alternative P2Y12 Inhibitors). We created propensity scores for each treatment regimen and assessed in-hospital stroke/death and bleeding complications using inverse probability of treatment weighted log binomial regression, with ASA-only as the reference group and adjusting for intraoperative protamine use and drain placement. We also assessed outcomes stratified by preoperative symptom status.

RESULTS: Of 195,619 CEA patients: 53% received ASA-only, 11% No-antiplatelet, 6% Clopidogrel-only, 30% DAPT, and 1% Alternative-DAPT. The corresponding unadjusted rates of in-hospital stroke/death were 1.3%, 1.7%, 1.2%, 1.2%, and 1.6%. After adjustment, compared with ASA-only, in-hospital stroke/death was lower with Clopidogrel-only (RR 0.81, 95% CI 0.67-0.97) and DAPT (RR 0.79, 95% CI 0.72-0.87). In symptomatic patients (26% of the cohort), there was a trend towards lower in-hospital stroke/death with DAPT (RR 0.88, 95% CI 0.76-1.00). In asymptomatic patients, in-hospital stroke/death was lower with Clopidogrel-only (RR 0.69, 95% CI 0.52-0.90) and DAPT (RR 0.73, 95% CI 0.64-0.83). Bleeding complications were higher with DAPT (RR 1.49, 95% CI 1.35-1.66) and trended toward higher with Clopidogrel-only (RR 1.22, 95% CI 1.00-1.48) but were similar across other regimens.

CONCLUSIONS: Compared with ASA-monotherapy, Clopidogrel-monotherapy and DAPT were associated with lower rates of in-hospital stroke/death after CEA driven by lower rates of stroke, albeit with higher rates of bleeding complications, particularly with DAPT. These findings highlight Clopidogrel-monotherapy as a potential alternative to DAPT for patients undergoing CEA, with similar efficacy and more acceptable bleeding risk. Analyses in patients on alternative P2Y12 inhibitors were limited by sample size; however, analyses with a larger cohort will be valuable in the future. Overall, our findings emphasize a potential role for clopidogrel-monotherapy in stroke prevention among patients undergoing CEA and highlight the importance of individualized risk assessment.

priorityArticles.title: Predicting Morbidity, Mortality, Revision, and Ambulation in Patients Undergoing Major Lower Limb Amputation for Peripheral Arterial Disease or Diabetes Mellitus: The Case for Regional Level Clinical Prediction Models.
priorityArticles.abstract:
OBJECTIVE: Several outcome prediction tools exist to support decision making for patients undergoing major lower limb amputation (MLLA). However, most predict a single outcome, are derived from registry level data, and lack external validation. The present study aimed to develop clinically focussed, multi-outcome prediction tools using granular regional data with immediate external validation on an international database.

METHODS: This study involved development, and internal and external validation of multivariable binomial and multinomial regression prediction models. All patients undergoing MLLA for ischaemic or diabetic indications between 1 January 2013 and 1 July 2023 at a single regional vascular hub were used for model development. Clinically focussed logistic multivariable binomial and multinomial regression models were developed predicting 30 day and 1 year mortality and revision, 30 day major morbidity or mortality, and best mobility achieved (binary and 3 category). Model complexity, crossvalidated receiver operating curve (ROC) discrimination and calibration were assessed and optimised, with the best performing models undergoing external validation on PERCEIVE study data. External validity was assessed using discrimination and calibration statistics, with one revision attempt permitted.

RESULTS: The development dataset included 609 patients (75.2% men, median age 69 years). Internal crossvalidated ROC values were 0.774 for 30 day mortality, 0.752 for 1 year mortality, 0.679 for 30 day revision, 0.707 for 1 year revision, 0.699 for 30 day major morbidity or mortality, 0.876 for binary best ambulation, and 0.752 for 3 category best ambulation predictions. All models were well calibrated. On external validation the ROC values were 0.616, 0.722, 0.617, 0.488, 0.697, 0.643, and 0.602, respectively.

CONCLUSION: The prediction models performed well for internal "regional" patient outcomes, especially for mortality and ambulation. On external validation, like other models externally validated on the PERCEIVE data, they failed to generalise to the wider population undergoing MLLA, except for 1 year mortality. Predicting patient outcomes from pre-operative variables remains challenging; however, regional level modelling may provide better performance over more general prediction tools.
